paras: The burning of the Scott home and expulsion of the Scott family from Salina, Kansas, took place on the night of December 27, 1881, when a mob set fire to the house of Mrs. Scott, a Black woman, and ordered her to leave town with her daughters. The family went to Denver, where the Denver Star took up the case as an outrage left unpunished because of their color.

According to the Star, two of Mrs. Scott's three daughters had been seduced by two white men 'said to be prominent citizens of Salina,' and when she threatened to prosecute, the men threatened the family with bodily injury unless it left town. She refused, began arranging a suit for damages, and turned down an offer of money to drop the matter.

On the night of December 27 a mob surrounded the family's cottage, set it on fire, and ordered Mrs. Scott out of town; the house was completely destroyed. Fearing the authorities would not protect them, the family accepted tickets and left for Denver.

The Star wrote that the Salina Herald had denounced the arson, but that the authorities had been 'lukewarm' and had made no attempt to find the perpetrators. Mrs. Scott was said to have retained an attorney to sue the town authorities and the two men; no report of arrests or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Saline County Journal made no mention of a fire, but two days after it noted that 'Madam Scott, accompanied by her troupe,' had left for Colorado: 'Good riddance to bad, very bad rubbish.' Its link to this family rests on the name, the timing and the destination.

The case reached a wider readership through the Indianapolis Leader, a weekly addressed to 'every colored man who favors the elevation of his race.' On February 4, 1882, a brief said the family had fled to Denver 'to save their lives' and that 'Short work ought to be made of these scoundrels.' A week later the Leader reprinted the Star's account under the headline 'INFAMOUS. Judge Lynch Badly Needed.' The Star itself argued that had Mrs. Scott been white the two men 'would have been lynched,' and it called them 'Negro-haters.'

reader.title: Burning of the Scott home and expulsion of the Scott family from Salina, Kansas
bases: A mob burned the family's house and ordered the mother to take her daughters and leave town, and the family left for Denver (A3); the Leader said they went to save their lives (A2).

The only account of the threat and the burning is the Denver Star article reprinted in the Leader (A3); the Leader's earlier brief (A2) appears to rest on the same Denver source, and the Salina Journal item (A1) mentions only a departure for Colorado.

accounts.label: Denver Star (reprinted by the Indianapolis Leader)
accounts.gist: Two white men who had seduced two of Mrs. Scott's daughters threatened the family and offered money; when she refused, a mob burned her house on the night of Dec. 27 and ordered her out of town, and the family took tickets to Denver.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Leader brief
accounts.gist: Mrs. Scott and her three daughters were 'most fouly outraged' by 'prominent (?) white citizens' and went to Denver to save their lives.

accounts.label: Saline County Journal (local)
accounts.gist: Reported only that 'Madam Scott' and 'her troupe' had departed for Colorado, calling it 'Good riddance to bad, very bad rubbish.'

framing.detail: The Salina paper in the coverage said nothing of a fire and mocked the departure of 'Madam Scott' and 'her troupe' as 'Good riddance to bad, very bad rubbish' (the Salina Herald, by contrast, is said to have denounced the arson).

The Indianapolis Leader, a weekly addressed to 'every colored man,' headed its reprint 'INFAMOUS. Judge Lynch Badly Needed.' and said Kansans should 'take law in their own hands' if the perpetrators went unpunished.

versions.value: Mrs. Scott and her three daughters
'three helpless colored women' (Leader preface) and 'two daughters' seduced (Denver Star text)

conflicts.note: Not a real contradiction: the Denver Star says Mrs. Scott came to Denver 'with her three daughters' and that two of them had been seduced; the Leader's preface counts three women.

versions.value: Living 'quietly and respectably' in a cottage paid for with the mother's savings
'Madam Scott' and 'her troupe,' 'bad, very bad rubbish'

conflicts.note: The local Journal item does not mention the fire and its identification with this family is inferred from the name, the date two days after the fire, and the destination.

record_check.record: Threat by two white men; 'The threat is dated only to before the arson.'

sources.note: Local item two days after the fire: 'Madam Scott, accompanied by her troupe, has departed for Colorado... Good riddance to bad, very bad rubbish.' No mention of a fire or threat; identification with this family is probable from name, date and destination but not certain.
quotes: We understand that Madam Scott, accompanied by her troupe, has departed for Colorado. She will star it in the provinces. Good riddance to bad, very bad rubbish.
